prompt: Which three accountabilities make up a Scrum Team in the 2020 guide?
hint: There is no manager among them.

choices.text: Project manager, team lead and developers
choices.why: Scrum has neither a project manager nor a team lead; their work is split among the three.

choices.text: Product Owner, architect, testers and developers
choices.why: Testers are Developers in Scrum, and there is no architect accountability.

choices.text: Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers
choices.why: Right. Three accountabilities, one team, no sub-teams.

choices.text: Sponsor, Scrum Master and Developers
choices.why: The sponsor is a stakeholder, not part of the Scrum Team.

prompt: Every backlog decision the Product Owner makes is reversed by a director who never attends. What does the lesson conclude?
hint: Who answers for the value of the product?

choices.text: The director is acting as Scrum Master
choices.why: The Scrum Master looks after the process and does not order the backlog.

choices.text: The Developers should order the backlog instead
choices.why: Ordering the backlog is the Product Owner's accountability.

choices.text: That person is not really the Product Owner
choices.why: Right. Others may influence the order by convincing the Product Owner; overruling them means someone else owns the product.

choices.text: It is normal, since the guide makes the Product Owner a committee
choices.why: The guide says the opposite: one person, not a committee.

prompt: What does the Scrum Master not do, by the guide?

choices.text: Make sure the events happen and are useful
choices.why: That is squarely their accountability.

choices.text: Assign tasks to the Developers
choices.why: Right. The Developers plan their own work; the Scrum Master coaches and removes impediments.

choices.text: Remove impediments that slow the team down
choices.why: Removing impediments is one of the jobs the guide gives them.

choices.text: Help the organisation understand Scrum
choices.why: That is part of establishing Scrum, which they do.

prompt: Put Scrum's events in the order they happen within one Sprint.
hint: Planning opens it; the retrospective closes it.
trap: The review comes before the retrospective: first what was built, then how the team worked.

prompt: How many minutes does the guide allow for the Daily Scrum?
hint: Same time and place every working day.

prompt: Who can cancel a Sprint, and when?
hint: Only one accountability has the authority.

choices.text: The Scrum Master, whenever the team falls behind
choices.why: Falling behind is a reason to renegotiate scope, not to cancel.

choices.text: The Developers, when an item is bigger than estimated
choices.why: They renegotiate scope with the Product Owner and keep the goal.

choices.text: Any stakeholder who attends the review
choices.why: Stakeholders influence the backlog; they do not control the Sprint.

choices.text: The Product Owner, if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete
choices.why: Right. The goal is the reason the Sprint exists, so only its loss justifies stopping it.

prompt: A team releases a fix to users on the Wednesday of a two-week Sprint. A manager says it should have waited for the Sprint Review. Who is right, by the 2020 guide?

choices.text: The manager, because the Scrum Master owns release dates
choices.why: No accountability in Scrum owns release dates that way.

choices.text: The team: releasing before the review is allowed
choices.why: Right. The review inspects the outcome with stakeholders; it does not gate releases.

choices.text: Neither: releases happen only at the end of the Product Goal
choices.why: Releases are not tied to the Product Goal.

choices.text: The manager: nothing ships until the stakeholders approve it at the review
choices.why: That turns the review into a gate, which the guide says it is not.

prompt: Why does the figure give Product Backlog refinement no box of its own?
hint: Compare it with the five events.

choices.text: It is done by the stakeholders after the review
choices.why: The Scrum Team refines the backlog.

choices.text: It is an ongoing activity, not an event
choices.why: Right. It happens whenever needed and has no time box.

choices.text: The 2020 guide removed refinement from Scrum
choices.why: Refinement is still in the guide, as an activity.

choices.text: Refinement happens only during Sprint Planning, inside its box
choices.why: It happens throughout the Sprint, not only at planning.

prompt: Match each artefact to its commitment.
Half way through a Sprint, an item turns out twice as big as expected. What does a Sprint Goal let the team do?
hint: Without a goal, success means finishing every item.

choices.text: Trade scope and still meet the goal
choices.why: Right. The goal is the objective; the items are one way to reach it.

choices.text: Lower the Definition of Done for that item
choices.why: Quality does not decrease during a Sprint.

choices.text: Extend the Sprint by a week to fit the item
choices.why: Sprints have a fixed length; the next one starts when this one ends.

choices.text: Cancel the Sprint and plan again
choices.why: The goal is not obsolete; nothing justifies a cancellation.

prompt: What does it mean that the Product Backlog is ordered rather than merely prioritised?
hint: Can two items share a place?

choices.text: Items are sorted by the date they were added
choices.why: Order reflects value and need, not arrival.

choices.text: Items are grouped into high, medium and low
choices.why: That is prioritising into bands, which allows ties.

choices.text: There is a first item, a second and a third; none share a place
choices.why: Right. 'High priority' for twenty items says nothing about which comes first.

choices.text: The Developers vote on the order each Sprint
choices.why: The Product Owner orders the backlog.

prompt: Which of these is a line for a Definition of Done rather than an acceptance criterion?
hint: One applies to every item; the other to one item.

choices.text: Reminders are sent by SMS the day before
choices.why: Behaviour of one feature, not a quality rule for all.

choices.text: A patient can cancel up to 24 hours before the appointment
choices.why: That says what one item must do: an acceptance criterion.

choices.text: The whole automated test suite passes
choices.why: Right. It applies to every item, whatever the item does.

choices.text: The booking screen shows the clinic's opening hours
choices.why: Specific to one feature, so an acceptance criterion.

prompt: An item meets its acceptance criteria but has not been reviewed, and review is in the Definition of Done. What happens to it at the end of the Sprint?

choices.text: It counts as done, since it does what was asked
choices.why: Doing what was asked is half; the Definition of Done is the other half.

choices.text: It is shown at the review marked as 'nearly done'
choices.why: Only work that meets the Definition of Done is shown.

choices.text: It counts as half its points in the velocity
choices.why: Points are counted for done items only.

choices.text: It goes back to the Product Backlog
choices.why: Right. It is not shown at the review and is reconsidered later.

prompt: An organisation wants every change to keep the p95 response time under 300 ms. Where does the lesson suggest putting that rule so that it applies without a separate task each time?

choices.text: In the Definition of Done
choices.why: Right. Then every item must meet it to count as done.

choices.text: In the acceptance criteria of the next performance story
choices.why: That covers one story; the rule must hold for every change.

choices.text: In the Sprint Goal of every Sprint
choices.why: The Sprint Goal is the objective of one Sprint, not a quality rule.

choices.text: In a performance-testing phase before each release
choices.why: That adds a phase; the lesson wants it inside 'done'.

prompt: The Agenda team committed 34 points to a ten-day Sprint. By how many points a day does the ideal line fall?
The burndown is flat on day 3, yet everybody worked hard that day. What is the most accurate reading?

choices.text: The chart was not updated
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson's reading is about what a burndown counts.

choices.text: Work was done but no item reached Done
choices.why: Right. A burndown counts finished items, so partly finished work shows nothing.

choices.text: Scope was added that day
choices.why: Added scope makes the line fall more slowly or rise, and the burndown hides it; a flat day says nothing finished.

choices.text: The team did nothing that day
choices.why: The question says they worked; the chart only counts what finished.

prompt: Which chart shows a scope change in the middle of a Sprint that a burndown would hide?

choices.text: The Sprint Backlog sorted by points
choices.why: A list, not a chart over time.

choices.text: A velocity chart across the last eight Sprints
choices.why: Velocity is per Sprint; it cannot show a change inside one.

choices.text: A burn-up
choices.why: Right. Work completed and total scope are separate lines, so a jump in scope is visible.

choices.text: A burndown with a steeper ideal line
choices.why: The ideal line does not record scope changes.

prompt: How many of the 34 committed points met the Definition of Done in the Agenda team's Sprint?
Match each failure to the symptom the lesson names.
hint: Each has a symptom visible from outside.

pairs.right: People look at one person while they speak
"I need to check" answers most questions
Points rise while delivery stays the same

prompt: A team's burndown is flat for eight days and drops in a cliff on the last two, while the testers work overtime every second Thursday. What is it?

choices.text: A healthy Sprint with a strong finish
choices.why: Everything finishing at the end is the problem, not strength.

choices.text: A small waterfall inside the Sprint
choices.why: Right. Analysis, coding and testing in sequence; finishing items one or two at a time is the fix.

choices.text: A Product Owner acting as a proxy
choices.why: That shows up as slow answers, not as a flat burndown.

choices.text: Velocity being used as a target
choices.why: Inflation shows in points per item, not in the shape of one Sprint.

prompt: What makes a retrospective change something, according to the guide's remedy?

choices.text: Holding it every day instead of once a Sprint, while problems are fresh
choices.why: It happens once per Sprint, at the end.

choices.text: The improvement goes into the next Sprint Backlog with an owner
choices.why: Right. Then it is work, not a conversation.

choices.text: Listing at least ten ideas each time
choices.why: Ten ideas that nobody does change nothing.

choices.text: Inviting the stakeholders so that management hears the complaints
choices.why: The retrospective is for the Scrum Team.

prompt: The team cannot estimate an item because nobody knows whether the calendar library handles recurring appointments. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Move it to a separate architecture phase before Scrum
choices.why: The lesson rejects a separate phase; the spike fits the backlog.

choices.text: Ask the Scrum Master to decide
choices.why: The Scrum Master looks after the process, not technical choices.

choices.text: A spike: a short, time-boxed investigation
choices.why: Right. It answers the question so the item can be estimated.

choices.text: Estimate it as large and see what happens
choices.why: A guess with no knowledge behind it is what the spike avoids.

prompt: Which decisions does the lesson say deserve a deliberate decision in the first Sprints? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The colour of the buttons
choices.why: Cheap to change later, so it waits.

choices.text: The boundaries between services
choices.why: Yes: redrawing them touches everything.

choices.text: How identity works
choices.why: Yes: every feature depends on it.

choices.text: The wording of error messages
choices.why: Cheap to change; leave it until the team knows more.

choices.text: The data store
choices.why: Yes: moving data later is expensive.

prompt: An architect serves four Scrum teams. What does the lesson warn them against?

choices.text: Becoming a gate every item has to pass
choices.why: Right. Decisions should be recorded and shared, not made a queue.

choices.text: Writing architecture decision records
choices.why: The lesson recommends them.

choices.text: Attending refinement sessions
choices.why: Refinement is where design is decided; attending it is the job.

choices.text: Talking to the Product Owners
choices.why: They decide the order the design work gets.

prompt: A Sprint lasts one ___ or less.
Sprint Planning answers three questions. Put them in the order the guide gives them.
items: What can be done this Sprint?
How will the chosen work get done?
trap: Why comes before what: the Sprint Goal guides which items are selected.

prompt: A team keeps a burndown that always reaches zero, yet stakeholders say every review is disappointing. What is the most likely gap?

choices.text: The items finished are not the ones that serve a goal
choices.why: Right. Quantity left says nothing about whether the right work was done.

choices.text: The ideal line is drawn wrongly
choices.why: A wrong ideal line would not make reviews disappointing.

choices.text: The Daily Scrum is too short
choices.why: Fifteen minutes is the rule; length is not what reviews reflect.

choices.text: The Sprints are too short to reach zero
choices.why: They reach zero; the problem is what they reach it with.
